Expat’s remote surgery medtech scores $92 million Series B for stroke care
Remedy Robotics just banked $92m to make remote stroke surgery real.
Simon Thomsen
Nov 17, 2026
2 min read
Share
0
Prefer Startup Daily
Remedy Robotics founder Dr David Bell. Image: supplied
Remedy Robotics, a San Francisco medtech treating stroke patients remotely, and cofounded by Perth-born doctor David Bell, has raised US$62 million (A$92m) in a Series B, backed by a range of Australian venture funds.
US venture firm DCVC led the round, with existing backers Blackbird, Tony Fadell’s Build Collective, Divergent Capital and KdT Ventures chipping in alongside the the University of California’s investment office, Skip Capital and super fund Hostplus as new investors.
Remedy previously raised US$35 million across its Seed and Series A rounds.
The fresh capital is for a clinical trial across the University of California’s network by a surgical robot designed to let specialists treat stroke patients hundreds of kilometres away. The medtech is seeking US Food and Drug Administration approval for procedures on the blood vessels supplying the brain. It also plans to place prototype robots with clinical partners, including the Australian Stroke Alliance.
Bell spent eight years in medicine, including cardiac surgery and air retrieval, before studying at Stanford, where he met his cofounder and CTO Jake Sganga. In 2021, the pair lined a garage in Venice Beach with lead, bought a second-hand X-ray machine and had a colleague in Berkeley operate their prototype remotely.
“This funding will allow our world-leading hardware, software, and machine learning teams to progress the N1 system towards clinical trials and potential FDA approval, while also developing additional features including full autonomy,” Sganga said.

The N1 robot lets a specialist at a console steer a catheter through a patient’s blood vessels. Its software uses machine learning to analyse scans, simulate procedures and match a 3D map of the vessels to live X-ray images. The team is also developing autonomous functions.
In August 2025, a Toronto neurosurgeon used the N1 to perform diagnostic angiograms on two patients at a hospital 6km away. A clinical team stayed with each patient while Pereira guided the catheter to check for narrowed or blocked vessels.
The N1 has yet to secure approval for routine clinical use anywhere. In Australia, Remedy and the Stroke Alliance want specialists in major cities to be able to remove a clot while the patient is still at their regional hospital.

Daylight Lands $80 Million for AI-Powered Security Operations
The company plans to accelerate product development, hire new talent, expand its US presence, and enter new markets.
By
Ionut Arghire
|
November 12, 2026 (8:12 AM ET)
Flipboard
Reddit
Whatsapp
Whatsapp
Email
Israeli-American cybersecurity startup Daylight has raised $80 million in a Series B funding round that brings the total raised by the company to $120 million.
The investment round was led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives’ Growth Equity, with additional support from Okta Ventures, Bain Capital, Craft Ventures, Vintage Partners, and Maple Capital.
Founded in 2024, with headquarters in New York and Tel Aviv, Daylight has built Aura, an AI-native platform that hunts for, analyzes, and contains cyber threats in real time.
Combining AI automation with human expertise, the platform continuously builds, runs, and customizes agents that handle day-to-day operations based on customers’ workflows, risks, and priorities.
Daylight provides these capabilities as part of a flexible service model. Customers can select the service to be fully managed, co-managed, or supported by forward-deployed engineers.
As AI agents handle routine operations, customers can use Aura to investigate their security environments, access security data, and manage security operations.
Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.
Daylight also covers AI platforms that organizations use, offering protection against prompt injection, risky MCPs, and rogue AI-driven activity.
“As these agents become more capable, they’ll fundamentally change how threats are detected, investigated, and contained, with expert security engineers implementing, governing, and continuously improving their operations,” Daylight co-founder and CEO Hagai Shapira said.
“At Daylight, we’re already bringing this vision to life through an agent-native model that combines the speed and scale of AI with the judgment and oversight of human experts. We’re building the foundation for a new era of security operations,” Shapira added.
The company plans to use the fresh funding to accelerate its platform’s development, expand its security and technology teams, grow its presence in the US, and enter new markets in the EMEA and APAC regions.

Israeli Cybersecurity Startup Daylight Raises $80 Million in Series B
The company combines AI agents with human security experts to automate threat detection and response, bringing its total funding to $120 million
Mandi Kogosowski
|
15/11/2026
Sponsored
Illustration: Tima Miroshnichenko via pexels.com
Israeli-founded cybersecurity company Daylight has raised $80 million in a Series B round led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives, bringing its total funding to $120 million. The New York-based company combines AI agents with human security specialists to detect, investigate, and respond to cyber threats.
The round included new investor Okta Ventures and existing investors Bain Capital, Craft Ventures, Vintage Partners, and Maple Capital. Daylight said its revenue grew more than 40-fold over the past year, driven by demand from Fortune 500 companies and AI-focused businesses. Its customers include Miro, LastPass, Lovable, Rogo, and dLocal.
Daylight's model addresses a growing challenge for corporate security teams: the increasing volume and complexity of threats, alongside difficulties recruiting and retaining experienced cybersecurity professionals. Its platform uses AI agents to handle routine security operations, while human engineers oversee investigations and decisions requiring specialist judgment.
The company offers fully managed and jointly operated services, as well as engineers who work directly within customers' security teams. According to Daylight, its system can detect threats within seconds and contain them within minutes, up to ten times faster than traditional managed security providers.
Its platform also monitors risks associated with enterprise AI adoption, including prompt injection attacks, insecure Model Context Protocol (MCP) connections, and unusual AI-driven activity.
Daylight was founded by Hagai Shapira and Eldad Rudich, who met while serving in an elite Israeli military intelligence unit. Shapira previously held a product leadership position at cybersecurity company Torq, while Rudich was Torq's first employee and vice president of research and development .
The company plans to use the new investment to expand its U.S. operations, enter additional markets in Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia-Pacific, and grow its engineering and technology teams.

articles.title: As AI Threats Surge, Daylight Raises $80M Led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives
articles.snippet: As AI Threats Surge, Daylight Raises $80M Led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives The Globe and Mail
articles.text:
NEW YORK CITY, NY / ACCESS Newswire / November 10, 2026 / Daylight, which combines AI agents with human security experts to detect, investigate, and respond to cyber threats, today announced an $80 million Series B led by Growth Equity at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, with existing investors Bain Capital, Craft Ventures, Vintage Partners, and Maple Capital. The round brings Daylight's total funding to $120 million. Daylight's revenue has surged more than 40x over the past year, fueled by rapidly growing demand from Fortune 500 enterprises and leading AI-native companies. Its customer base includes Lovable, LastPass, Rogo, dLocal, and Miro.
October's wave of cyber incidents, dubbed "Black October," stretched incident response teams already under pressure from increasingly complex security threats. As organizations turn to AI to help manage these mounting demands, the technology isn't necessarily easing the burden. A July 2026 ISC2 survey found that 65% of cybersecurity professionals using AI now spend more time determining whether to trust its recommendations than they did a year ago, while 63% spend more time verifying its outputs.
The challenge goes beyond AI adoption. Companies also struggle to find security services that fit their specific needs. Traditional managed security providers offer rigid, one-size-fits-all services, while standalone AI tools often leave companies managing yet another system. Some organizations want to outsource security operations entirely, while others have internal teams and want to retain control over their detections and processes. As a result, enterprises are left piecing together multiple vendors for detection and response, threat hunting, phishing, data protection, and security data management.
Daylight brings these capabilities together through a flexible service model that combines AI automation with some of the world's top security engineering talent, expertise that most companies struggle to recruit and retain. Its AI-native platform and security engineers continuously build, run, and customize AI agents to each customer's systems, workflows, risks, and priorities. The agents handle day-to-day security operations, while engineers focus on decisions requiring human judgment. Customers can choose how the service is delivered, whether fully managed, co-managed alongside their internal teams, or supported by forward-deployed engineers.
Daylight detects threats in seconds and responds to and contains them within minutes, up to 10 times faster than traditional managed security providers. Customers can run leaner security teams without sacrificing the expertise needed to protect their businesses, as AI agents take on routine operations and experienced security engineers handle complex decisions. Through Aura, Daylight's AI-native platform, customers can also investigate their security environment using natural language, access their security data in a centralized data lake, and manage their security operations from one place.
Daylight's coverage also extends to the AI platforms enterprises use themselves, protecting against AI-native risks like prompt injection, risky MCPs, and unusual AI-driven activity. Those detections run through Daylight's full MDR workflow, where AI activity is investigated alongside identity, endpoint, cloud, SaaS, and business context. The capability is already in use by enterprise customers, including Miro.

articles.text:
Project Omega Raises $80 Million To Develop Nuclear Fuel Recycling Infrastructure
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 11:10 PM
Project Omega Raises $80 Million To Develop Nuclear Fuel Recycling Infrastructure
Project Omega has raised $80 million in Series A financing to develop nuclear fuel recycling infrastructure and long-duration power products. B Capital led the round, with participation from noa VC, 645 Ventures, and other investors focused on nuclear technology and national security. Existing investors Starship Ventures, Mantis Ventures, Decisive Point, Virta Ventures, Pace Ventures, Essential Capital, and Washington Harbour Partners also participated.
B Capital General Partner Jeff Johnson will join Project Omega’s board of directors.
The company is developing a non-aqueous pyroprocessing platform intended to recover useful materials from spent nuclear fuel. Its technology targets isotopes that can be used in long-duration power systems, reactor feedstock, and commercial, scientific, and medical applications.
Project Omega said the process does not separate pure plutonium and could reduce nuclear-waste volume by up to 90%.
Its initial products include radiovoltaic systems that convert the natural decay of radioisotopes directly into electricity. Potential applications include sensors, autonomous systems, communications infrastructure, spacecraft, undersea platforms, and equipment deployed in areas where battery replacement is difficult.
Project Omega has worked with Idaho National Laboratory through the ARPA-E CURIE program and demonstrated stable electrical current from strontium-90 at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. It has also developed radioisotope power systems through DARPA’s Rads to Watts program.
The financing will support a pilot facility for isotope recovery and feedstock production, construction of a nuclear fuel recycling facility, and further development and manufacturing of the company’s X Series expeditionary power systems.
Project Omega has offices in Newport, Rhode Island, and Hailey, Idaho, along with a laboratory in Fall River, Massachusetts.
KEY QUOTES:
America’s growing demand for reliable power is colliding with a nuclear fuel cycle that remains dependent on foreign supply and leaves enormous value stranded in used fuel. Project Omega’s technology has the potential to create multiple revenue streams from a largely untapped domestic resource, spanning long-duration power, reactor feedstock and strategic isotopes. We’re excited to support Staff Sheehan and his highly experienced team as they scale this platform and unlock economic potential across the nuclear value chain.
Jeff Johnson, General Partner and Global Head of Energy at B Capital
The country’s nuclear renaissance will not happen without the fuel. We have a domestic source for this, nearly 100,000 metric tons of used nuclear fuel, which is one of America’s largest untapped energy resources. We are building a vertically integrated strategy around an abundant domestic feedstock, with a non-aqueous recycling process that recovers useful isotopes, and products with clear strategic demand. That combination creates the potential for an entirely new nuclear innovation economy.
Stafford Sheehan, Founder and CEO of Project Omega
